questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Where follow-up is incomplete, explain why the unobserved outcomes plausibly could or could not make an important difference to the approved estimate, rather than citing a small percentage alone. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

BACKGROUND
In patients with type 2 diabetes, inhibitors of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)
reduce the risk of a first hospitalization for heart failure, possibly through glucose-
independent mechanisms. More data are needed regarding the effects of SGLT2 in-
hibitors in patients with established heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction,
regardless of the presence or absence of type 2 diabetes.
METHODS
In this phase 3, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 4744 patients with
New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction
of 40% or less to receive either dapagliflozin (at a dose of 10 mg once daily) or pla-
cebo, in addition to recommended therapy. The primary outcome was a composite
of worsening heart failure (hospitalization or an urgent visit resulting in intravenous
therapy for heart failure) or cardiovascular death.
RESULTS
Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 pa-
tients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in
the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85;
P<0.001). A first worsening heart failure event occurred in 237 patients (10.0%) in
the dapagliflozin group and in 326 patients (13.7%) in the placebo group (hazard
ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.83). Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in
227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the
placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98); 276 patients (11.6%) and
329 patients (13.9%), respectively, died from any cause (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI,
0.71 to 0.97). Findings in patients with diabetes were similar to those in patients
without diabetes. The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal
dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups.
CONCLUSIONS
Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of wors-
ening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who
received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the
presence or absence of diabetes. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DAPA-HF ClinicalTrials
.gov number, NCT03036124.)

26|BACKGROUND
27|In patients with type 2 diabetes, inhibitors of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)
28|reduce the risk of a first hospitalization for heart failure, possibly through glucose-
29|independent mechanisms. More data are needed regarding the effects of SGLT2 in-
30|hibitors in patients with established heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction,
31|regardless of the presence or absence of type 2 diabetes.
32|METHODS
33|In this phase 3, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 4744 patients with
34|New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction
35|of 40% or less to receive either dapagliflozin (at a dose of 10 mg once daily) or pla-
36|cebo, in addition to recommended therapy. The primary outcome was a composite
37|of worsening heart failure (hospitalization or an urgent visit resulting in intravenous
38|therapy for heart failure) or cardiovascular death.
39|RESULTS
40|Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 pa-
41|tients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in
42|the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85;
43|P<0.001). A first worsening heart failure event occurred in 237 patients (10.0%) in
44|the dapagliflozin group and in 326 patients (13.7%) in the placebo group (hazard
45|ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.83). Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in
46|227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the
47|placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98); 276 patients (11.6%) and
48|329 patients (13.9%), respectively, died from any cause (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI,
49|0.71 to 0.97). Findings in patients with diabetes were similar to those in patients
50|without diabetes. The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal
51|dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups.
52|CONCLUSIONS
53|Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of wors-
54|ening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who
55|received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the
56|presence or absence of diabetes. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DAPA-HF ClinicalTrials
57|.gov number, NCT03036124.)

5|arge clinical trials involving pa-
6|tients with type 2 diabetes have shown that
7|inhibitors of sodium-glucose cotransporter
8|2 (SGLT2) reduce the risk of hospitalization for
9|heart failure.1-4 Most patients in these trials did
10|not have heart failure at baseline, so the benefit
11|of treatment with an SGLT2 inhibitor largely re-
12|flected the prevention of incident heart failure.
13|The reduction in the risk of hospitalization for
14|heart failure was observed early after randomiza-
15|tion, which raised the possibility of mechanisms
16|of action that differed from those usually postu-
17|lated to explain the cardiovascular benefits of
18|glucose-lowering therapies.5-9 In addition to di-
19|uretic and related hemodynamic actions of SGLT2
20|inhibitors, effects on myocardial metabolism, ion
21|transporters, fibrosis, adipokines, and vascular
22|function have also been proposed.5-9 These actions,
23|along with preservation of renal function, would
24|also benefit patients with established heart fail-
25|ure, including those without diabetes, in whom
26|SGLT2 inhibitors have not been tested.4,10,11 We
27|designed the DAPA-HF (Dapagliflozin and Pre-
28|vention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure)
29|trial to prospectively evaluate the efficacy and
30|safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor dapagliflozin in
31|patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection
32|fraction, regardless of the presence or absence of
33|diabetes.12,13
34|Methods
35|Trial Design and Oversight
36|The executive committee designed and oversaw the
37|conduct and analysis of the trial in collaboration
38|with the sponsor, AstraZeneca.12,13 The trial was
39|conducted and reported in accordance with the
40|protocol and the statistical analysis plan, both of
41|which are available with the full text of this ar-
42|ticle at NEJM.org. The trial was approved by the
43|ethics committee at each center. The safety of
44|patients in the trial was overseen by an indepen-
45|dent data and safety monitoring committee. The
46|analyses conducted by the sponsor were replicated
47|by an independent academic group at the Univer-
48|sity of Glasgow. The first draft of the manuscript
49|was prepared by the first author, who had unre-
50|stricted access to the data, and was reviewed and
51|edited by all the authors. All the authors made the
52|decision to submit the manuscript for publication
53|and vouch for the accuracy and completeness of
54|the data and for the fidelity of the trial to the
55|protocol.
56|Patients
57|Eligibility requirements included an age of at least
58|18 years, an ejection fraction of 40% or less, and
59|New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II, III,
60|or IV symptoms. Patients were required to have
61|a plasma level of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic
62|peptide (NT-proBNP) of at least 600 pg per mil-
63|liliter (or ≥400 pg per milliliter if they had been
64|hospitalized for heart failure within the previous
65|12 months). Patients with atrial fibrillation or
66|atrial flutter on baseline electrocardiography were
67|required to have an NT-proBNP level of at least
68|900 pg per milliliter, regardless of their history
69|of hospitalization for heart failure.

71|failure device therapy (an implantable cardiovert-
72|er-defibrillator, cardiac resynchronization thera-
73|py, or both) and standard drug therapy, including
74|an angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitor, an
75|angiotensin-receptor blocker, or sacubitril-valsar-
76|tan plus a beta-blocker, unless such use was con-
77|traindicated or resulted in unacceptable side ef-

30|Statistical Analysis
31|We calculated that 844 primary outcome events
32|would provide the trial with a power of 90% to
33|detect a hazard ratio of 0.80 for the comparison
34|between dapagliflozin and placebo, using a two-
35|sided alpha level of 0.05. With an expected an-
36|nual event incidence of 11% in the placebo group,
37|we estimated that the enrollment of approximately
38|4500 patients would provide the required num-
39|ber of primary events, based on an anticipated
40|recruitment period of 18 months and an average
41|follow-up period of approximately 24 months.
42|We used a closed testing procedure, with pre-
43|specified hierarchical testing of the primary and
44|secondary outcomes. The type I error was con-
45|trolled at a two-sided alpha level of 0.0499 for
46|multiple comparisons across primary and second-
47|ary outcomes, with one interim efficacy analysis
48|taken into account.

50|had undergone randomization in the analyses of
51|the primary and secondary outcomes, according
52|to the intention-to-treat principle. Baseline char-
53|acteristics were summarized as means and stan-
54|dard deviations, medians and interquartile ranges,
55|or percentages. We used a mixed model for re-
56|peated measurement to analyze longitudinal mea-
57|sures (e.g., glycated hemoglobin level and body
58|weight) and estimated the least-squares mean dif-
59|ferences between treatment groups, together with
60|95% confidence intervals. Time-to-event data were
61|evaluated with the use of Kaplan-Meier estimates
62|and Cox proportional-hazards models, stratified
63|according to diabetes status, with a history of hos-
64|pitalization for heart failure and treatment-group
65|assignment as fixed-effect factors; for the renal
66|outcome, the baseline eGFR was included instead
67|of a history of hospitalization for heart failure.
68|We used the Cox models to calculate hazard ratios,
69|95% confidence intervals, and two-sided P values
70|and used a semiparametric proportional-rates
71|model to calculate total (including recurrent)
72|events.16

75|as a composite, rank-based outcome, incorpo-

evidence.quote:
Missing data and informative censoring
The time-to-event analysis using the Cox regression depends on the assumption of non-
informative or ignorable censoring, corresponding to the missing-at-random assumption. The
missing data in this context are patients who are prematurely censored due to WoC, LTFU or
otherwise incomplete follow-up of endpoints. The amount of missing data will be described
eg, in terms of the number of patients and patient time with incomplete follow-up as described
in Section 4.1.5.
Patient retention and follow-up are at the forefront of study planning and conduct, and the
amount of incomplete follow-up is expected to be small. To assess the impact of missing data
and the robustness of the results with regard to the assumption of non-informative censoring,
sensitivity analysis will be planned based on the evaluation of the missing follow-up and
discussed in relation to the observed efficacy signal. This may include analysis where
scenarios in terms of increased risk in censored patients are explored to identify a 'tipping
point' where statistical significance would be lost.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Where follow-up is incomplete, explain why the unobserved outcomes plausibly could or could not make an important difference to the approved estimate, rather than citing a small percentage alone. Relate the reported extent to the outcome event scale or variability and any known follow-up timing or reasons; retain what is unknown. For time-to-event estimates, event counts contextualize scale but do not by themselves mathematically bound the hazard ratio or its interval. A calibrated probable judgment can rest on nearly complete outcome accounting without exact censoring times or a formal sensitivity analysis. Missing reasons or timing alone do not require no_information; judge whether available circumstances support a reasonable inference.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

BACKGROUND
In patients with type 2 diabetes, inhibitors of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)
reduce the risk of a first hospitalization for heart failure, possibly through glucose-
independent mechanisms. More data are needed regarding the effects of SGLT2 in-
hibitors in patients with established heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction,
regardless of the presence or absence of type 2 diabetes.
METHODS
In this phase 3, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 4744 patients with
New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction
of 40% or less to receive either dapagliflozin (at a dose of 10 mg once daily) or pla-
cebo, in addition to recommended therapy. The primary outcome was a composite
of worsening heart failure (hospitalization or an urgent visit resulting in intravenous
therapy for heart failure) or cardiovascular death.
RESULTS
Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 pa-
tients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in
the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85;
P<0.001). A first worsening heart failure event occurred in 237 patients (10.0%) in
the dapagliflozin group and in 326 patients (13.7%) in the placebo group (hazard
ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.83). Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in
227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the
placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98); 276 patients (11.6%) and
329 patients (13.9%), respectively, died from any cause (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI,
0.71 to 0.97). Findings in patients with diabetes were similar to those in patients
without diabetes. The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal
dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups.
CONCLUSIONS
Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of wors-
ening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who
received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the
presence or absence of diabetes. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DAPA-HF ClinicalTrials
